title: The services page a manufacturer actually needs
metaTitle: A manufacturer services page that works
excerpt: List each service in the buyer's words, with an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. A grid of vague capabilities does not help someone send a drawing.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen, for a piece on making a services list easy to scan.
caption: A quiet corridor with clear rooms. A services page should be that easy to read. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a manufacturer name a service?
faqs.answer: Use the words a buyer already says when they request a quote. Process names and product names beat internal department titles. If sales says one phrase on the phone, the page and the spec file should use that same phrase.

faqs.question: What is a useful boundary on a service?
faqs.answer: A concrete limit. Materials, sizes, file types, and the work you decline. A buyer with the wrong part can leave early, and a buyer with the right part can see that you know your own edge. Flexibility without a range is not a boundary.

faqs.question: How many services should the page list?
faqs.answer: As many as are truly distinct, often six to ten, with the one you want inquiries for placed first. If the list is longer, group it under process headings. Repeating one process under several industry names makes the page longer and less clear.

markdown:
A manufacturer services page is a list of work in the buyer's language. A buyer who needs specs and confidence is scanning for an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. The next step is to talk to sales or download a spec. A grid of vague capabilities, quality, partnership, innovation, does not give them any of the three.

Treat each service as a small offer. Someone should be able to read one block and know what they would leave with, what you will not take on, and how to start. If a block cannot say those three things, it is a slogan, and it should come off the page.

## Name the work the way it is purchased

Use the words a buyer already types and already says to a salesperson. CNC milling, laser cutting, contract sewing, board assembly, label converting, powder coating. The internal department name can stay on the org chart. The page should use the name that matches a request for quote.

Group the list by the way buyers arrive. By process, when they know the operation. By product family, when they know the object and are looking for who can make it. By industry only when the constraint is truly different, such as a cleanroom step or a traceability pack. An industry menu that repeats the same three processes under five vertical names is a longer page with less information.

Lead with the service that should earn the next serious inquiry. The rest can follow in a plain order: most requested, or the sequence of the process itself. Alphabetical order is a fallback for a long list of peers. It is a poor way to rank a short list where one capability pays for the building.

Write the opening of the page as a key to the list. One or two sentences on what you make and who the list is for. Then the services. A long introduction about being a solutions provider delays the only content the buyer came to read.

## Outcome, boundary, and the next step

Each service block needs an outcome the buyer can picture. Finished housings, kitted and labeled. Panels cut, edged, and ready for their hardware. Garments sewn to a graded spec and packed by store. The outcome is the thing that arrives at their dock or their next process. It is the result of the work.

Each block needs a boundary. Materials you run, sizes you can hold, files you accept, and the work that belongs to a different kind of shop. A boundary is a favor. It stops a buyer with the wrong part from spending a week in qualification. It also tells the right buyer that you understand the edge of your own process. Shops that claim every material and every geometry are hard to trust with a specific one.

Each block needs a next step, and it should be the same kind of step across the page. Talk to sales, or download the spec for that service. The link can differ. A machining block can point at a machining spec. A finishing block can point at a finish card. The action stays recognizable. A buyer should not have to learn a new ritual for every row.

Write the three parts in that order, in short paragraphs or a short labeled stack. Outcome. Boundary. Next step. A person comparing two suppliers can scan the boundaries and the files. A person who already knows you fit can take the step without rereading the philosophy.

## What a boundary sounds like when it is real

A useful boundary is concrete. "Aluminum and stainless, prototype through production, drawings in STEP or a dimensioned PDF." "Cotton and wool programs, cut-and-sew, minimums stated on the pricing page." "We coat parts that arrive finished-machined. We do not fabricate the part." The reader can sort themselves.

A weak boundary hides inside a positive claim. "We support a wide range of applications." "Our team is flexible on specifications." Those sentences feel helpful in a conference room. On the page they tell a buyer nothing about whether to send the file. Replace them with the range you want, and with the range you would rather refer elsewhere.

If you decline work, you can say so once, in a calm line under the list. No design-from-scratch, no repair of damaged customer tools, no materials outside the published list. You do not need to be stern. You need to be findable. The buyers you want will read it as competence.

Standards and certifications belong on the service they actually cover. A general ISO mark in the corner of every block, with no scope, becomes wallpaper. If the certification covers the coating line and not the machine shop, attach it to the coating line. A buyer who needs confidence is allowed to ask where the certificate applies. Answer it before they ask.

## Services are distinct from markets

A market page and a service page do different jobs. The service page says what you do to the object. A market page, if you need one, says which constraints show up in that market: documentation, cleanliness, seasonal deadlines, the way orders repeat. Mixing them into one grid produces blocks that all sound the same, with a different industry noun swapped in.

If a single process serves three markets, keep one service block and mention the markets inside the boundary. "Used on outdoor equipment, instruments, and low-volume vehicle programs." That is enough. Three blocks that repeat the same equipment list waste the minute a buyer will spend.

Applications can be links from the service, for a buyer who needs to see a cousin of their part. Those links should land on proof with a constraint and a decision, which is a different page. The services page stays a map of work. It should not become a scrapbook of every job you have liked.

## Make the page something sales can send

The best test is forwarding. A salesperson should be able to send one service block to a new contact and have it stand alone. The block names the work, the edge, and the file. The buyer can read it on a phone between meetings. If the block only makes sense after a tour of the homepage, it is still a fragment of a brochure.

Keep the names stable. The phrase on the services page, the phrase in the spec file name, and the phrase sales uses on the phone should match. "Precision metalwork" on the site and "the CNC cell" in the quote is a small crack, and small cracks are where confidence leaks. Pick the buyer's phrase and use it in all three places.

Download links should be real. A spec per service, or one spec with anchored sections, is fine. A single corporate PDF that never mentions the service by name is a dead end. Put the revision where a buyer can see it. Stale specs are a trust problem, and they are an operations problem. Someone has to own the swap when a tolerance or a material list changes.

Hanabi designs and builds this kind of page so the blocks stay editable by the people who know the work. The structure is ordinary on purpose. Outcome, boundary, next step, repeated cleanly. The visual system can be quiet. The words do the selling. Selected projects on the studio site show the same bias toward a clear offer. You can look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and see how a public page carries a specific object and a specific decision, which is the standard these service blocks should meet.

## Order, length, and the first screen

On a phone, the first screen of this page should show the key sentence and the start of the first service. The first service should be the one you want. Everything above it is a tax. A full-bleed photograph of the plant, a rotating banner, and a paragraph of welcome copy will push the list down until the buyer has to hunt.

Six to ten blocks is enough for most contract manufacturers. If you have more, group them under process headings so the page has a table of contents. A single endless stack of peer blocks makes people miss the one they came for. A filter helps only when the list is truly long and the filter words match the buyer's words.

Cross-link the pricing shape where the boundary mentions money, minimums, or tooling. The services page does not need to repeat the whole price model. It needs to avoid contradicting it. If the machining block says low volume welcome and the pricing page says fifty-piece minimums, fix the disagreement before you publish either.

## A review you can do in one sitting

Read every block out loud and mark any sentence that could move to a competitor's site unchanged. Those sentences come out. Then mark any block that lacks a boundary. Those get a boundary or they leave the page. Then click every spec link. Then ask someone who writes quotes whether they would forward the page.

[Google's helpful-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a useful external check. People-first pages make clear who is responsible and help the reader do the thing they came to do. A services page passes when a stranger can tell what you make, what you will not make, and how to start. It fails when the page could belong to any plant with a camera.

The about page is where that "who" becomes specific. After the work is listed, a buyer who is still unsure will look for the people who stand behind it. [How a manufacturer should write an about page](/blog/how-a-manufacturer-should-write-an-about-page) is the next piece, because the origin story only earns its place when it changes the decision to talk to sales or download a spec.
